prompt: What's a common feature of literary postmodernism?
options: Irony, metafiction, fragmentation, mixing high and low culture, suspicion of grand narratives
correctAnswer: Irony, metafiction, fragmentation, mixing high and low culture, suspicion of grand narratives
explanation: The label has been more useful for grouping than for defining. Many writers called postmodernist (Pynchon, Barth, Calvino, Borges) reject or modify the label. Postmodernism covers very different writers and modes.

prompt: Whose 1979 The Postmodern Condition gave the philosophical sense of postmodernism as 'incredulity toward metanarratives'?
explanation: Lyotard argued the grand stories modernity told about itself — progress, science, Marxism, Christianity, the Enlightenment — had lost their unquestioned authority. What replaced them was a plurality of smaller narratives, each with limited claims.

prompt: Fredric Jameson's 1991 book gave postmodernism its most influential cultural-political analysis: Postmodernism, or, the Cultural Logic of Late _________.
explanation: Jameson argued postmodernism wasn't just a style but the cultural logic of late capitalism: pastiche replacing parody, depthlessness replacing depth, schizophrenic time replacing linear narrative. The book provided a vocabulary for thinking about post-1960s culture in relation to economic conditions.

prompt: What did David Foster Wallace's 1993 essay 'E Unibus Pluram' attack and propose?
options: It attacked postmodern irony as exhausted and called for new sincerity
correctAnswer: It attacked postmodern irony as exhausted and called for new sincerity
explanation: The post-2000 'New Sincerity' movement (Wallace, George Saunders, Dave Eggers) tried to write past postmodern detachment. Other proposed replacements: metamodernism, post-postmodernism, digimodernism. Postmodernism's specific moment (1960s-90s) has passed; its techniques persist in transformed forms.

prompt: Match each post-postmodern proposal to a description:

pairs.right: Wallace, Saunders, Eggers; writing past postmodern irony

explanation: By the 2000s many critics were arguing postmodernism had ended. The honest assessment: postmodernism's specific moment has passed, but its techniques and concerns persist in transformed forms. The label has become historical rather than current.

prompt: Which Argentine writer's 1940s short fictions (Ficciones, The Aleph) created templates much subsequent experimental fiction would draw on?
explanation: Borges (1899-1986) wrote almost no novels. His fictions are short — 5-15 pages — and densely conceptual. He went blind in middle age, worked as a librarian. He never won the Nobel — a long-running scandal of the prize.

prompt: In Borges's 'Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote,' what does Menard do?
options: Recompose chapters of Don Quixote word-for-word, which the narrator judges richer than Cervantes's for being written in the 20th century
correctAnswer: Recompose chapters of Don Quixote word-for-word, which the narrator judges richer than Cervantes's for being written in the 20th century
explanation: Each Borges story takes a single conceptual idea and works it out as fiction with extraordinary economy. 'The Library of Babel,' 'The Garden of Forking Paths,' 'Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius,' 'The Aleph' all do similar work.

prompt: Mexican novelist Juan _________'s Pedro Páramo (1955), a short novel told through fragmentary voices including the dead, is foundational for magical realism.
explanation: Other Latin American precursors: Adolfo Bioy Casares (The Invention of Morel anticipated virtual reality), Alejo Carpentier (coined 'lo real maravilloso'), Julio Cortázar (Hopscotch, 1963 — readable in multiple orders).

prompt: What postmodern moves did Borges introduce that became staples?
options: Metafiction, erudition as fiction (invented references), conceptual compression, genre dissolution
correctAnswer: Metafiction, erudition as fiction (invented references), conceptual compression, genre dissolution
explanation: Almost every postmodern writer has read Borges. Calvino, Eco, Pynchon, Auster, Bolaño all show his influence directly. Latin American writers anticipated and shaped what would become postmodern technique decades before North American postmodernism named itself.

prompt: Match each Borges story to its conceptual idea:

pairs.right: The universe as a library containing every possible book
Time as branching alternatives, every choice splitting the universe
An imagined world's encyclopedia begins to replace the real one

explanation: The Spanish-language publishing industry was integrated across countries, supporting regional literary movements. The 'Boom' of the 1960s exported these techniques globally.

prompt: Whose 1973 Gravity's Rainbow is the canonical American postmodern novel?
explanation: Thomas Pynchon (b. 1937), 760 pages, set during and after WWII, organised around the V-2 rocket, with hundreds of characters and constant philosophical-historical-conspiratorial digression. Pynchon has been famously reclusive. His writing — comic, paranoid, dense, allusive, deeply musical — sits at the centre of what 'postmodern fiction' came to mean.

prompt: What did John Barth's 1967 essay 'The Literature of Exhaustion' argue?
options: The realist novel had used up its possibilities; new fiction would have to operate self-consciously about its own conditions
correctAnswer: The realist novel had used up its possibilities; new fiction would have to operate self-consciously about its own conditions
explanation: Barth (1930-2024) was the theorist of American metafiction. His novels — The Sot-Weed Factor (1960), Giles Goat-Boy (1966), Lost in the Funhouse (1968) — practised what the essay preached. Robert Coover and William Gass belong to the same metafictional moment.

prompt: Don DeLillo's 1985 novel about a college professor's family disoriented by media saturation and an 'airborne toxic event' is _________ Noise.
explanation: White Noise crystallised the postmodern sense of dread-and-detachment. DeLillo's later novels include Libra (1988, on Lee Harvey Oswald) and Underworld (1997), an 800-page sweep through American Cold War decades — many critics' pick for the great late-20th-century American novel.

prompt: David Foster Wallace's 1996 Infinite Jest combined Pynchonian length with what ambition?
options: Explicit New Sincerity ambitions against postmodern irony
correctAnswer: Explicit New Sincerity ambitions against postmodern irony
explanation: By the 1990s a generation came of age in dialogue with Pynchon, DeLillo, and Barth. Wallace's New Sincerity attempted to write past postmodern detachment. Jonathan Franzen, Jennifer Egan, Colson Whitehead, George Saunders continued postmodern moves in transformed form.

prompt: Match each American postmodern novel to its author:
explanation: The big-American-postmodern novel as a recognisable type has faded. Its techniques (metafiction, paranoia, genre play) survive in many contemporary writers, just no longer as a programmatic movement. The category has been criticised for its narrow demographic (mostly white male).

prompt: Whose 1967 One Hundred Years of Solitude defined what international readers expected of Latin American fiction for thirty years?
explanation: Gabriel García Márquez (1927-2014, Nobel 1982) traced the Buendía family across a century in the fictional town of Macondo. The book combines realist family-saga structure with elements of myth, magic, and folk legend. Sold tens of millions worldwide.

prompt: What's magical realism?
options: Mode in which the magical is treated as ordinary, the ordinary as wondrous; events violating physical laws narrated in matter-of-fact prose
correctAnswer: Mode in which the magical is treated as ordinary, the ordinary as wondrous; events violating physical laws narrated in matter-of-fact prose
explanation: The mode has roots in Carpentier and Rulfo but reached widest audience through García Márquez. Subsequent magical-realist writers in many countries — Rushdie, Toni Morrison, Allende, Murakami in some moods — work in the lineage García Márquez popularised.

prompt: Julio Cortázar's 1963 novel readable in numerical order or in a sequence the author provides is _________.
explanation: Cortázar (1914-1984) also wrote masterly short stories (Bestiary, End of the Game, Blow-Up). Mario Vargas Llosa (Nobel 2010) wrote tighter, more political, more realist work than García Márquez: The Time of the Hero, Conversation in the Cathedral, The War of the End of the World.

prompt: Which post-Boom Chilean writer wrote against the Boom — against magical realism, against its commercial template?
explanation: Roberto Bolaño (1953-2003): The Savage Detectives (1998), 2666 (2004 posthumous). His mode: long, dark, formally restless. Latin American fiction continued after the Boom but shifted modes. Clarice Lispector, César Aira, Mariana Enriquez, Samanta Schweblin operate in modes the Boom didn't anticipate.

prompt: Match each Boom novelist to a defining work:
explanation: Each had a distinctive style. The grouping was partly publishing convenience — they were translated and marketed together. Latin American literature is no longer reducible to the Boom; the continent continues to produce major writing in many idioms.

prompt: Which German-born writer (lived in England) used long sentences, unbroken paragraphs, and black-and-white photographs in works including The Rings of Saturn and Austerlitz?
explanation: Sebald (1944-2001) wrote in German. Genre-blurring — part novel, part essay, part travelogue, part memoir. His subject is largely the Holocaust and what survived of European Jewish life — handled obliquely. He died in a car accident at 57. Brief output, outsized influence.

prompt: Karl Ove Knausgaard's six-volume autofictional My Struggle (2009-11) totals approximately how many pages?
explanation: One of the major autofictional projects in literary history. Extreme detail of his actual life — childhood, his alcoholic father, marriage, fatherhood. Annie Ernaux (Nobel 2022) is a parallel autofictional project; The Years (2008) traces French collective experience from 1941 to 2006. Other major autofiction: Cusk, Heti, Lerner, Nelson, Offill.

prompt: The pseudonymous Italian author of the four Neapolitan Novels (My Brilliant Friend etc., 2011-2014), a global phenomenon with over 16 million copies sold, is Elena _________.
explanation: Lila and Elena from childhood in 1950s Naples through old age. The novels demonstrate that traditional realist long-form fiction, done with sustained intelligence about gender and class, can still command global readership. The author has remained pseudonymous despite intense journalistic investigation.

prompt: What's clear about the contemporary literary novel?
options: No single dominant mode — multiple traditions coexist; literary fiction more global than ever
correctAnswer: No single dominant mode — multiple traditions coexist; literary fiction more global than ever
explanation: Major writers come from everywhere. Translation has expanded as a cultural enterprise. Prize culture (Booker International, Neustadt, Nobel, National Book Award translated category) directs attention beyond major-language markets. Han Kang's 2024 Nobel illustrates the global pattern.

prompt: Match each contemporary writer to a description:

pairs.right: Genre-blurring; long sentences with photographs; oblique Holocaust meditation
Polish novelist; Nobel 2018; Flights, The Books of Jacob
Korean novelist; Nobel 2024; The Vegetarian, Human Acts

explanation: Whether the contemporary moment will retrospectively look like a coherent period — like 'modernism' or 'the Boom' — or like fragmentation without single direction is unanswerable from inside it. The 21st century is being written.
